'''Giuseppe Melfi''' (June 11, 1967) is an [[Italy|Italo]]-[[Switzerland|Swiss]] mathematician who works on [[practical number]]s and [[modular form]]s.

==Career==
He gained his PhD in mathematics in 1997 at the [[University of Pisa]]. After some time spent at the [[University of Lausanne]] during 1997-2000, Melfi was appointed at the [[University of Neuchâtel]], as well as at the [[University of Applied Sciences Western Switzerland]] and at the local University of Teacher Education.

==Work==
His major contributions are in the field of [[practical number]]s. This prime-like sequence of numbers is known for having an asymptotic behavior and other distribution properties similar to the sequence of [[Prime number|primes]]. Melfi proved two conjectures both raised in 1984:<ref>Margenstern, M., ''Résultats et conjectures sur les nombres pratiques'', C, R. Acad. Sci. Sér. 1 299, No. 18 (1984), 895-898.</ref> the first one states that every even number is a sum of two practical numbers, a property that is still unproven for primes. The second one is that there exist infinitely many triples of practical numbers of the form <math>m-2,m,m+2</math>. He also proved that there exist infinitely many [[Fibonacci sequence|Fibonacci numbers]] that are practicals<ref>{{cite journal|title=A survey on practical numbers |author=Melfi, G. |journal=Rend. Sem. Mat. Torino |volume=53 |year=1995 |pages=347–359 |url=http://www.seminariomatematico.polito.it/rendiconti/cartaceo/53-4/347.pdf}}</ref>

 

Another notable contribution has been in an application of the theory of [[modular forms]], where he found new [[Eisenstein series|Ramanujan-type identities]] for the [[divisor function|sum-of-divisor functions]]. His seven new identities extended the ten other identities found by Ramanujan in 1913.<ref>Ramanujan, S., ''On certain arithmetical functions'', Transactions of the Cambridge Philosophical Society, 22 (9), 1916, p. 159-184.</ref> In particular he found the remarkable identity
:<math> \sum_{\stackrel{0< k< n}{k\equiv1\bmod3}} \sigma(k)\sigma(n-k)=\frac19\sigma_3(n) \qquad \mbox{  for }n\equiv2\bmod3</math>
where <math>\sigma(n)</math> is the sum of the divisors of <math>n</math> and <math>\sigma_3(n)</math> is the sum of the third powers of the divisors of <math>n</math>.

In 1996 [[Paul Erdős]] wrote him two letters<ref>{{cite web|url=http://members.unine.ch/giuseppe.melfi/erdos1.jpeg |title=Erdős, P., 19th March 1996|access-date=2026-04-02}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://members.unine.ch/giuseppe.melfi/erdos2.jpeg |title=Erdős, P., 29th May 1996|access-date=2026-04-02}}</ref> in which several problems were proposed. They met in [[Eger]] in July
<ref>
{{cite book|last1=Györy|first1=Kálmán|last2=Pethö|first2=Attila|last3=Sós|first3=Vera T.|title=Number Theory: Diophantine, Computational, and Algebraic Aspects|url=https://books.google.ch/books/content?id=QBvwioC6cQcC&pg=PR10&img=1&zoom=3&hl=en&sig=ACfU3U34VpXyzccmtLqNsSxEpRLgkdkHlA&w=1280|year=1998|publisher=World Scientific|isbn=3-11-015364-5|page=x-xvii}} 
</ref>
, but Erdős died in September. In the subsequent decade Melfi studied some [[Paul Erdős#Erdős's problems|Erdős problems]] with some notable contribution<ref>{{cite journal
  | last =Bloom
  | first =T. F.
  | title =Erdős Problem #124
  | journal = Erdős Problem
  | url=https://www.erdosproblems.com/124
  | access-date =2026-04-02
  }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal
  | last =Bloom
  | first =T. F.
  | title =Erdős Problem #125
  | journal = Erdős Problem
  | url=https://www.erdosproblems.com/125
  | access-date =2026-04-02
  }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal
  | last =Bloom
  | first =T. F.
  | title =Erdős Problem #470
  | journal = Erdős Problem
  | url=https://www.erdosproblems.com/470
  | access-date =2026-04-02
  }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal
  | last =Bloom
  | first =T. F.
  | title =Erdős Problem #876
  | journal = Erdős Problem
  | url=https://www.erdosproblems.com/876
  | access-date =2026-04-02
  }}</ref> in particular concerning [[sum-free sequence]]s.

Among other problems in elementary [[number theory]], he is the author of a theorem that allowed him to get a 5328-digit number that has been for a while the largest known primitive [[weird number]]. Since 2019, with a 14712-digits primitive weird number, he shares this record, with a team of collaborators.<ref>Amato, G. Hasler, M.F., Melfi, G. and Parton, M. ''Primitive abundant and weird numbers with many prime factors'', 
Journal of number theory 201 (2019), 436-459.</ref>

In applied mathematics his research interests include [[probability]] and [[simulation]].
